Introduction of	bills-Mr.	Reid-Bill
intituled: "An Act to amend the Bank of Canada Act."

subtopic: RULING OP MR. SPEAKER ON MOTION FOR INTRODUCTION OF BILL BY PRIVATE MEMBER
speechtext:
When the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) on Wednesday last moved for leave to introduce a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act, a point of order was raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and I deferred my decision until to-day because I wanted to make a complete examination of the proposed bill. I find that the bill is not in order, and shall now give the details of my decision.
The objects of the bill which the hon. member for New Westminster is seeking to introduce in amendment to the Bank of Canada Act are to allow the Bank of Canada to hold silver coin and bullion in conjunction with gold as a reserve against the note issue and deposit liabilities and also to authorize the issue of certificates against the silver held in the reserve.
Under section 31 of the act, the Receiver General of Canada is entitled to share in the profits of the bank. If the reserve required as security against outstanding notes and deposit liabilities is to consist of silver bullion as well as gold, the fluctuations in the price of silver may cause the bank to sustain serious losses and therefore its profits may be substantially curtailed with an accompanying reduction of the receiver general's share therein and therefore a diminution of the public revenue. It is an established principle in British parliaments, which was set down by a standing order passed in the British House of Commons as far back as 1707, that financial business must originate in a committee of the whole house.
Private members cannot introduce a bill of this character, which ought to be preceded by a resolution on motion of a minister with the recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General.
Moreover, there is now on the order paper a resolution in the name of the Minister of Finance antecedent to a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act so as to increase the capital stock of the bank and to assure ownership of a majority of shares by the government. Full discussion on this measure cannot be anticipated by a private member's bill, and in determining whether a discussion is out of order on the ground of antici-

pation, the authors say that regard shall be had by the Speaker to the probability of the matter anticipated being brought before the house in a reasonable time. I am well aware that a motion for leave to bring in a bill is in order even if another similar motion with regard to a bill dealing with the same- subject matter stands on the order paper, but when the latter is a government measure announced in the speech from the throne and bound to be taken up by the house, I doubt if the discussion of some of its provisions can be forestalled by the introduction of a private member's bill. For this reason and also because the bill sought to be introduced deals with a part of the dominion's finances, I rule it out of order.

subtopic: RULING OP MR. SPEAKER ON MOTION FOR INTRODUCTION OF BILL BY PRIVATE MEMBER
speechtext: Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I suppose I shall have to abide by your decision, but I would point out that your decision dealt with only one part of the bill. When this bill was before the house last year the same position was taken by the then Speaker, and although I have modified my bill to conform with the ruling then given, it has again been thrown out, and again only the first clause of the bill has been dealt with. Last year when I introduced my bill I was supported by members of the present government who said that the bill was in order.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to
do more than suggest to the government, particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the possibility of considering whether parliament might not itself take some steps to mark its appreciation of the heroic efforts of those who restored to society the two gentlemen who were entombed at Moose River. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to my right hon. friend that had I been in the house yesterday I would have sought to give expression to what I believe to be the feelings of all hon. members with respect to the heroic service rendered by those who participated in effecting the deliverance of Doctor Robertson and Mr. Scadding from their long entombment in the mine at Moose River. Unfortunately I was not in the city. I sent a message by wire, however, from Toronto, to the Premier of Nova Scotia, in which I ventured to express sentiments on behalf of all members of parliament which I believed it would be their wish to have expressed. In the circumstances I did not rise in my place to-day on the orders of the day to make a further reference, but I may say to my right hon. friend that the government has had under consideration the very matter he has suggested.
Now that the leader of the opposition has mentioned the subject, I should like to say that I know it is the wish of hon. members of parliament that some expression should be given in its records to the feelings of relief, joy and thankfulness felt by us all at the saving of the lives of Doctor Robertson and Mr. Scadding, to our feeling of profoundest sympathy with Mrs. Magill and the members of her family in the bereavement which they
Supply-Superannuation

have suffered, and to our unbounded admiration of the heroism of those who, altogether regardless of the risks involved, cooperated in the rescue effected.
I imagine at no other time have the thoughts of persons of all classes in all parts of this country been more united in their hopes and wishes and prayers than they have been during the -past fortnight. There has been on the part of the people of Canada as a whole a unanimity of feeling alike of the deepest sympathy and of the greatest admiration as respects those who displayed such determination, fortitude and endurance and who so bravely and so efficiently cooperated in effecting the rescue, as also with respect to those who were rescued. We have felt that we have had a manifestation of the human spirit at its highest and best. That spirit has exhibited itself in a manner which has reflected credit not only on all those who participated in the actual rescue, but on our whole country. There has been service, not for the sake of recognition or decoration, but for the love of service itself; a willingness, if need be, to give life with no thought other than to save life. It is wholly appropriate that members of this parliament should express their profound appreciation of what will remain I believe for all time an epic in Canadian annals, revealing at its true worth the character of the men and women of this country.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps fools rush in where angels fear to tread. This example of bravery and endurance has thrilled all Canada, but I am concerned, sir, with the value of human life wherever it may be, whether in Canada or in Ethiopia, and I think it is time that the Christian nations of the world woke up to the value of human life anywhere.

This is one of the matters to which we gave some attention and made some reference during the first year we were in office. It is possible there may be an increase in our liability as the fund may or may not be ample for the purpose of meeting the charges which may be made against it. Supply-Post Office

Perhaps the
minister has some general observations to make regarding the department.

This item is made up of salaries of postmasters of post offices on the city or 6taff basis, of district directors and superintendents of postal services. It is practically all outside service. It includes the salaries of 1,143 railway mail clerks, the mileage allowance paid railway mail clerks and any salaries of the temporary staff in the outside service, totalling 430 employees. Then there are railway mail services amounting to $6,718,'474 and steamboat, $272,241. I think those are the general services that are provided for.

Prior to the Easter recess
when some other items of the Post Office Department were under consideration I raised the general question as to why we should not have a sort of concise balance sheet to show exactly how the post office is run and what its annual income and expenditures really are. At present hardly a member of the house knows anything about the operations of the postal service. We skip from one page of the estimates to another, discussing one item and then something else without really getting a complete picture of the operations of the postal service of Canada. When it comes to the buildings we find that they are in some way included as part of the operations of the postal service, though coming I understand under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works. It is impossible for any member to know exactly what the net result is. I asked the minister a few weeks ago whether he would prepare a statement along these lines and I should like to have from him now, or at any rate later on in the estimates, a complete statement such as any business organization would give in the discussion of the operations of an ordinary utility. That is to say, I want to know the total amount of income in the last fiscal year, the total expenditures, what buildings come under the jurisdiction of the department and whether the operations of these buildings are charged to the post office account. We should know all that. I wonder if the minister is in a position to give that information.

I thought
that I gave that information at the last sitting of the committee but evidently I did not make it sufficiently detailed for the hon. gentleman to get the plan clearly. The total revenue for the fiscal year just ended was $39,122,198. From that is taken first the amount of salaries and allowances paid
[Mr. J. C. Elliott.1
to postmasters at revenue offices, being $6,171,000. You add to that other things such as discount, stamp vendors and postmasters, compensation to messengers for special delivery of letters, $302,000. Then there are losses by fire, burglary and so on amounting to $4,000; balance of commission paid to other countries on money order business, $7,000; postage on parcels to other countries, $56,764; transit charges on correspondence to other countries; $55,000; indemnity paid owners of lost insured parcels, $18,000. These items make a total of $6,614,000.
I am not surprised that any hon. member should have some difficulty in understanding why the bookkeeping is done in the way it is, but that has been the system since confederation, I am advised. All the revenues are put into one account and that comes to $39,000,000 odd as we figure it at the present time. Then you deduct from that the $6,000,000 for the items I have already mentioned-$6,614,748.40. That leaves what is called a net revenue-it is so described, and has been for as many years as I have been able to find any details of it-amounting to $32,507,449.64. The expenditure for the outside service is made up of salaries and allowances: to postmasters and staffs, $12,260,000; district directors and staffs, $810,000; railway mail clerks, $1,951,179; mileage for those clerks, $634,330; making a total of $15,655,509 for what are called salaries and allowances. Coming to the mail service: for railways we pay out $6,718,474; for steamboats, $272,241; for land services, which includes the rural mail deliveries and the side services, that is from station to office or distributing point, $5,945,150; air service, $281,483; mail bags, $220,000. That makes a total of $13,437,348. The balance of the $29,000,000 is made up of the following items: commissions to postmasters, $2,400; travelling expenses, $60,000; printing and stationery, $250,000; postage stamps, $185,000; hand stamps, $388,000; Magdalen Islands service, $500; compassionate allowance, $1,000. Those items total $886,900. The total of that is $29,979,757.

That does not give us the
real picture of the postal service in this country. We have here a net income of a little over $32,000,000 and an expenditure of close to $30,000,000. That does not take into consideration all the buildings and equipment throughout the country?
No.

I do not think that is a
proper way to do the business of the country.

Supply-Post Office
If the only excuse the government has-and it applies to past governments as well-is that this system has been in effect from the time of confederation, I think it is high time we had a change, and I suggest that the Post Office Department cannot start too quickly to bring about a change by adopting some more modem method of doing its business than, evidently, it practises at the present time. There are throughout this country huge post offices; we do not know their value; we do not know the cost of maintenance of them or any of them, and we cannot have a real picture of the utility, as I call this postal service, until there is placed before us a proper balance sheet, showing the total income, the total expenditure, the cost of the various services that the people receive in respect of matters that come within the jurisdiction of the postal service.
I know that the present Postmaster General is just as anxious as any member of this house to see that we get an efficient and up to date postal service. I believe he wants to conduct the post office, as far as he possibly can, free from some of the evil influences which we know sometimes surround postmasters in their official positions. I want to impress upon him the desirability of instituting from now on a change in the whole administration of the post office. For instance, buildings are erected-by whom, I do not know; possibly by the Department of Public Works.
By the Department of Public Works.

Some are erected, I believe, by way of unemployment relief. Suddenly the Post Office Department is asked to take over these buildings, whether it requires them or whether it does not. Of course the buildings are maintained by the Department of Public Works and do not appear in any way as part of the postal service. I have come to the conclusion that as in fact they are part of the postal service they should come as far as possible within the jurisdiction of the Post Office Department; at all events they should not be entirely under the Department of Public Works. I favour, of course, the largest possible degree of cooperation between the two departments. But what I am anxious to have from the Postmaster General is some idea whether we cannot escape, from now on, from the tradition which has evidently affected the operation of the Post Office Department since the time of confederation, and launch out into some more up to date method of doing its business.

With regard to part, at any rate, of my hon. friend's statement I must say that he cannot get into any argument with me, because I agree that this is an unusual way of keeping the accounts. But when you come to consider the whole situation you are confronted with the problem of just in what way you can improve upon it. My hon. friend is quite right in saying that the expenditures include nothing for the construction of all the larger buildings that house the large post offices and post office facilities, departmental and other. They are built and to a large extent furnished by the Department of Public Works. They are taken care of by the same department. While perhaps it looks like an anomalous situation to have one department erecting the buildings and another department occupying them and not being charged up with anything for rental, for caretaking, or for a large part of the repairs, at the same time, as one who happens to know something about the Department of Public Works, I believe that that department should construct all the buildings that are used for the various services. I do not think that we should have the Post Office Department erecting buildings-
I am not suggesting it.

-and various other departments also constructing buildings. I believe it might be possible to keep some account of what it actually costs the country for reasonable rentals or a reasonable interest on the expenditure upon the buildings to which my hon. friend refers. I might add that when he asked the question the other evening I made inquiries of the Department of Public Works, which by the way is always a busy department, particularly so this year and at this time, when they are preparing their estimates, and my hon. friend might think I was exaggerating if I told him the amount of time required by a great many clerks to give us a fairly accurate estimate of what these costs are. Take the Langevin block, which was built by the Department of Public Works; this building is now occupied by various departments. At the present time it seems almost an interminable job to figure out the space occupied by each of these various departments in the various buildings throughout the country.
But surely any department store has to do that in figuring its costs.

My hon. friend would know as much as I know about the
Supply-Post Office

way in which a department store is run. I do not imagine that a department store, all owned by the same company, would require to figure out the cost of the foot space occupied by each little branch of each department.

I do not say that, but they actually do figure out how much of the cost should be allocated to each department, and the manager of that department is held responsible for making the department pay. With regard to the production even of locomotives, in the railway shops, or repairs, they have staffs that are able to figure the cost and that is charged up to the various departments, or so I am informed. I do not see why we cannot have in the government a system which would be in conformity with modern business practice.

I have no doubt it could be done; it is a question for parliament to consider. This is not a new matter; it has been considered many times before. It is just a question whether or not the cost of figuring out all these various services in the many buildings that would have to be taken into account can 'be justified as an expenditure at the present time. It would have to be a very greatly increased expenditure, and now, beyond question, we are facing a heavy deficit when you take into account the rental of the buildings at fair prices.
Just one other point, as a matter of information. In the statement he gave did the minister include the cost of the inside service, what we would call the overhead, the cost to the department?
No, that $29,975,000, to which I think my hon. friend refers, is just for the outside service.

I do not want the minister to feel for a moment that I am criticizing him personally or the officers of his department; this is something that has grown up during the years, and I can understand how difficult it would be to launch out immediately on something new after going along in the same old ruts for so many years. At the same time there is no reason in the world why the things I have suggested cannot be done. I think the people have a right to know exactly what the postal service is costing them, and we are not in a position to say what it really does cost.
Would the hon. member make that apply to all other departments?

Absolutely, without exception; I do not think we should make any difference between the departments. I should like every department to stand on its own feet. This should apply particularly to the Post Office

department because it is a utility, a revenue producing department. It may be that the people are not paying enough for the services that are rendered, but I should like some true idea of the real position of that utility, and under the present method of bookkeeping it is impossible to obtain that idea. To-day I do not know how many post office buildings are owned outright by the government. I do not know how many buildings are leased for postal purposes. I do not know, and I do not suppose the minister is in a position to give it to me at this time, the total cost of the buildings in various parts of this dominion that have been erected purely for postal purposes. We should have all that information; we should have some idea of the annual interest charges on those postal buildings, and we should have some idea of the cost of maintenance. When we get those facts we will have some idea of what the postal service of this country is costing us. As it is now all we receive is a bald statement, in more or less detail, that there is a net revenue of $32,000,000 and an expenditure of approximately $29,000,000. That is not a fair picture to present to the people, because it is not a true picture. All I am attempting to do this afternoon, as I have done previously, is to see whether it is not possible to assist the minister in getting a proper picture of the postal service of this country from a financial standpoint so that perhaps in another session we may be able to review the postal estimates more intelligently than we can at the present time. I cannot say anything more about it now, except that often after we go over these estimates we are no wiser than we were before, and that is unfortunate. Sometimes I cannot help thinking that it is odd that we in this little group, who are sometimes charged with knowing so little about business., should be the ones to insist on business methods being followed in the conduct of government.

I would only say to my hon. friend that it is not a matter of choice. From sheer necessity we are compelled to cut out some expenditures that we might think advisable at the present time, in arranging our estimates it has been necessary to do that. I did ask the public works department for a statement along the lines suggested by my hon. friend. When the hon. gentleman speaks of buildings used for post office purposes only, however, I think he will realize that very few of the public buildings that have been erected in Canada are used for postal purposes only. In nearly every building there is a customs office though unfortunately, in the interests of economy, many of those

Supply-Post Office
customs offices in the smaller places were closed recently. At other points you may have a little armoury in the public building, where the arms of the local militia unit are kept, and of course when you get into the larger buildings the situation becomes much more complicated.
I quite appreciate the fact that my hon. friend is doing this in a desire to be helpful, and I have no quarrel with him at all. I think all these discussions are entirely to the good, because this should be a business institution. The department is a large one; our revenue now amounts to nearly $40,000,000 a year, and comes principally from the sale of postage stamps. That means a lot of business, a great many transactions and a great deal of work in handling mail, newspapers and various other articles. My hon. friend will realize that even in the management of an office, for instance, the situation has changed materially in the last fifteen or twenty years.
I recall that when I first occupied an office no one ever thought of estimating the cost of the foot space occupied by each individual in the office. That is done to-day in up to date offices; they know just how much space is used by each man in the office, what share of the time of the office staff he requires, what is involved in the cleaning of his office space, and so on. I suppose the time will come, perhaps sooner than my hon. friend thinks, when some such system will be adopted in the various departments of the government. That is all I can say about it. I am satisfied the business of the department is being conducted with due consideration for economy and an endeavour to serve the public. I do not believe I can add anything to what I have already said.

Are there, individual
accounts for each post office in Canada, indicating the debits, credits and revenues of each?
Yes, and it is on those revenues that the remunerations of postmasters in revenue post offices are based. The annual report shows all post offices in Canada and the revenues of each.
Has the minister the net revenue for the Toronto post office?

For the year ended March 31, 1935, the revenue of the Toronto post office, including an amount of $17,169 for non-accounting suboffices, was $6,899,398.08. That is divided, and I can give the figures if the hon. member wishes to have them.
No; I should like to have the net profit over and above the expenses.
We have not that information. That revenue goes in as part of the $39,000,000, and there is no net expense account for Toronto.

How can you tell whether a post office is a liability or an asset to the country? I am referring now not particularly to the Toronto post office, but to any post office from which revenues are derived.

We can give the salaries and allowances, and can give further information as to costs of all services. We can give a close estimate of a particular office's proportion of the general overhead of the department.
Then I take it that the net revenue for Toronto is not kept separately.
No, in the sense that there is a charge for public buildings.

In looking over the public accounts I notice that in Toronto the head official is called a district director, whereas in Vancouver he is called a district superintendent. What is the difference between these two officials?

In some cases the offices of district director and postmaster for the main office have been combined, and in that event the official is called a district director, because he not only manages the local post office but also directs the services in the district. In the other instance the official is called a district superintendent. That is the best explanation I can give. I have had prepared a chart showing a list of offices and officials, starting with the office boys right up to superintendents.
Can the minister tell when the distinction was first made between district superintendent and district director?
The previous government did it.
I am advised it was about 1933 or 1934.
It was done by the Bennett government.

The public accounts show that the district director of Toronto receives only $4,771 per year. That seems to be a small salary for a man with such great responsibility. The district director in a large city like Toronto would have heavy responsibilities. Is that all he receives?
He has so little because McNaughton has too much.

The maximum to which he will eventually go will be $6,000. a substantial -sum.

Is the minister referring to the postmaster at Toronto?

I think we have had this
afternoon a demonstration of the fact that the system by which the Post Office Department is conducted is an antiquated one. I am not going to condemn either the present or the preceding Postmaster General, because they have all proceeded along the same line. It is antiquated, no matter how it originated, and it is time for a change. We do not know to-day whether the Post Office Department makes a million or loses ten millions; the only answer we can get from any postmaster general is that the total revenue is so much, because as to expenditures he knows nothing. What we need in Canada is a first class, up to date Public Works department. It is the largest spending department we have and there should be in it an efficient accounting system to keep track of all the work done for the Post Office Department. To begin with, it supplies that department with buildings and charges no rent. It furnishes the buildings, supplies the engineers, caretakers, firemen, cleaning staff and does all that work at the instigation of some postmaster in a particular place such as Toronto. If he wants to spend ten thousand or fifteen thousand dollars tearing down a wall here or there, the Public Works department is charged with that work and the Post Office Department pays nothing. The whole system should be changed so that we might know whether the department was making or losing money. Each department should stand on its own feet; that is the way business is done, and there would be no difficulty at all if such a system were carried out. If the Public Works department builds a post office in Toronto, say, costing $600,000, or a customs house, the Post 12739-137i
Office Department or the department for which the work is done should be charged at the rate of three or four per cent, just as I would be charged if I were occupying space in some store. That is the system followed by Eaton's and Simpson's in Toronto, and there is no reason why it could not be followed here. There is no reason in the world why the Postmaster General should not be in a position to answer one intelligent question-and as I say it is not his fault. The sooner we change the system the better it will be for the Post Office Department. That department should get down to a business basis and let us know whether it is making or losing money. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent in Toronto alone for the Post Office Department for which that department does not pay a red cent.
An observation was made about the salary which the director was receiving

they have a new name for the postmaster in Toronto. When Mr. Lemon was there he received seven or eight thousand a year as postmaster, and now we have a distinguished gentleman acting as superintendent. His official position is postmaster, and he has the superintendent's job, and I am told that he gets $4,771; yet the man is capable of making much more than that in a city like Toronto. I am not advocating high salaries because I cannot make any high salary myself-
Oh, oh.

-but I do think that
everyone should be treated fairly. My advice to the government is this: Never mind the past; forget about it altogether and get down to hardpan. Start a new system so that we shall know what we are doing and find out whether we are making or losing money in the Post Office Department. The Post Office Department can pay for aeroplanes without going to the Public Works department; they can subsidize a steamship company themselves and where the Public Works department does work for them they should be charged with it, and that money deducted from their total revenue. National is that it would clip about ten hours off the running time from Vancouver to Ottawa were it allowed to do so. I myself have left Ottawa on a train ten hours late and arrived on time in New Westminster. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I should like to see the Canadian National patronized, and when it comes to speed I do not think that there are any trains that can beat the Canadian National from Ottawa to Vancouver.

What has been the situation since Sir Henry Thornton retired from the presidency of the Canadian National and especially since the passing by the late administration of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act placing three trustees in charge, the chairman of which is Mr. Fullerton, whom I know very well, who lived in the city of Halifax and was a graduate of Dalhousie and a partner of the late Sydney Harrington, a queen's counsel of that day, one of the most outstanding members of the legal profession in Canada. The present condition, over which unfortunately this government has absolutely no control, is attributable to the late government, who saw fit to appoint these three trustees for ten years. They are removable only by an address of both houses and on specific charges, and that is why today the Canadian National is going behind and therefore protracting the running time of its trains. The Ocean Limited used to make the run from Halifax to Montreal in twenty-four hours and the Maritime Express made the run to Montreal in twenty-seven hours, leaving in the afternoon. I came up on that train the other day and to my amazement I found that the running time was thirty-six hours, as fixed by the special management under Mr. Fullerton and his associates, who do not know anything about the running of trains but can argue a case.
We are talking about post offices.

Hon. gentlemen opposite, now that they are relieved of responsibility, do

not hesitate to suggest reforms. I wonder why the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence), who sat in the house when his party was on this side, did not induce the government of those days to bring about the reforms he is suggesting to-day. My hon. friends opposite are pursuing a different method now from that which they followed when they were on the treasury benches. The Postmaster General referred a moment ago to the Atlantic service. I remember that in the days when Sir Henry Thornton was in control he made a running agreement with the Cunard line and the White Star line, whereby they carried freight which was handed over to the Canadian National system. Trade grew by leaps and bounds, and with it came the development of the port of Halifax, which did not interfere with the great sister port of Saint John, served by the Canadian Pacific railway. To-day what are the conditions? The Canadian Pacific boats, the Duchess boats and the Mont boats, running from Liverpool to Halifax with mail, hand it over to whom? To the Canadian National railway through to Montreal? No. That mail is handed over to the Canadian Pacific railway. These ships land only their passengers and mail, which are taken on the Canadian Pacific line with a Canadian National engine hauling the train. The ships go to Saint John to unload their freight, and then return to Halifax to pick up freight which, as it comes over the Canadian National system to Halifax as the last port of departure, they could not get otherwise. Now these new 10,000 ton freight boats drop into Halifax to land freight for the maritime provinces or for Nova Scotia; they then go round to Saint John and spend a week, and come back to Halifax to pick up freight. It seems to me that since these Canadian Pacific and Canadian National acts, legislation to repeal which has been introduced by the Minister of Railways, have been on the statute books, the Canadian National railway has been put in the lion's jaws and they are crushing it inch by inch. There is no better evidence of that fact than the propaganda which is received every day from Montreal, emanating from get-rich-quick gentlemen on a street that is very well known, St. James street, and from Wall street in the city of New York.
That is the condition that prevails to-day. Not even the Minister of Railways has power

May I say a word on behalf of those with whom I worked at the time I held the office of Postmaster General, and may I pay due credit to those men who under all governments in years gone by have given and even at the present time are giving their attention to the perfection of the postal service in Canada, and have brought it to its present state of development. It stands second to none in the world.

It is only fair to permit me to say a word, because this has been put over me several times in the House of Commons. It was put over me when I was criticizing the experimental farm. I have not criticized the service given by the Postmaster General. I talked about an antiquated system, the way business is done. The service of the men is perfect, and I do not want my hon. friend to think I am criticizing it. We are getting the best service the Post Office Department can give. I have to pay the present Postmaster General a compliment by saying that I believe he has a vision of the future better than some who think they have it, and he will get even a better service. He may adopt the system I have asked him to adopt, and may get a proper accounting system, get down to business and do business as business should be done.
You cannot divorce a man from the service.

I have been informed by an official of the Post Office Department that the salary of the postmaster in the town of Mont Joli in Rimouski is over $4,000 a year. If so, I suppose it is a post office which falls under the control of the civil service commission, as the salary comes above the $3,000 mark. Is there a rule of age, so far as this particular postmaster is concerned? Surely, if he comes under the control of the civil service commission, he should be retired at the age of sixty-five years. May I inform the minister that this postmaster is seventy-five years old, and if the minister will take the trouble to inquire in his own department I believe he will find there are special reasons why this office should be reclassified and a new appointment made.

To the hon. members for Parkdale and Gloucester may I say that I did not understand the hon. member for Parkdale to cast any reflection upon the people working in the service, or most certainly I would have said something in reply. The minister is right.

As the minister who is trying to administer the department and as one who realizes that he cannot learn all about it in a few months, I wish to pay tribute to the men who have occupied that position in the past. We have had a great many excellent postmasters-general and I know that in most cases they have done their very best and have given to the public a service that has not always been thoroughly understood or thoroughly appreciated.
There is a good deal to be said, I take it, for the view of the hon. member for Park-dale that this should be a paying service; that we should charge enough to make the various branches of the service pay their way. If ever there was a time in the history of this country when that was absolutely necessary this is that time. I assure my hon. friend and other members of the committee that in every branch of the service we are endeavouring to see what can be done that the charges we impose will more nearly meet the expenses which we are forced to incur.
In answer to my hon. friend from Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) with regard to postmasters under the civil service act, sixty-five years is the age limit, I understand.
At which they can stay in?

There is not, I understand, an age limit for retirement for
revenue postmasters; each case stands on its own merits.

Does the minister realize what he is saying? I said a moment ago that this post office is under the control of the civil service commission. The minister need not consult his officials because I know as much about the matter as they do. I would like this post office to be classified through the civil service commision, and once this classification has been made I think the postmaster who is above seventy-five years of age should be retired. If the minister wants a precedent I will give him one. In 1930 the post office at Rimouski was classified by the civil service commission and salaries fixed for the postmaster and his assistant, and the postmaster was retired. I want exactly the same precedence to be followed with regard to the Mont Joli post office.
Is the present postmaster Liberal or Conservative?
I have not the faintest idea. I know he is over age and is no good.
I will look into the matter and will see what can be done.

There are two
criticisms of the service which have been given me by certain business people. One is in regard to delay in delivering letters owing to holidays. In many places now Saturday is a half holiday; there is no delivery on Sunday, of course, and it is becoming the practice on a number of occasions to give a holiday on Monday, which means that the mail is not delivered for two and a half and sometimes three days. In the case of urgent business or sickness or anything of that kind that is a very long delay. Personally I do not want to see the men deprived of their holidays, but I think it might be possible by a slight increase of staff to arrange that there would not be that long delay.

I quite * agree with what my hon. friend has said. It is a difficult matter to weigh accurately against the inconvenience that may be caused by delay in delivering the mail the convenience of those who are working at its disposition. But complaints have been very few. Difficulty does arise in cases like armistice day when it falls on a Monday. There is the short day on Saturday, and then Sunday. Or take Good Friday, followed by a short day Saturday, and then Sunday and Easter Monday. We try to keep sufficient staff on during such holidays to give a reasonable service. We do not attempt to provide anything like the ordinary service, but we do provide a reasonable service. The question arises as to whether the ordinary employees should be brought back and paid overtime. At the present time it does not seem to be easy to pay overtime in connection with these matters, but it is possible we shall have to consider

a more strict insistence upon employees coming back on holidays such as Good Friday, Enster Monday and so on.

I had no intention of increasing the work of the employees, but I think in these cases the public is entitled to service. In the larger places it should be possible to have a reserve staff and it should not require a great number of people to give the service. Very frequently reserve teachers are carried on the staffs of our schools in case of sickness among the regular teachers, and possibly the same method could be followed here. Another question: Does the department use the different bus lines for the delivery of mail? I think we have all had some experience with the delivery of newspapers by buses. Very often these newspapers arrive at their destination some hours before the regular mail. Unless the department keeps up with the regularly accepted means of transit, it is going to be left behind.
What does the hon. member mean by bus lines?

I am referring to the passenger buses that are running all over the country. If the newspapers can make use of these buses for delivery purposes, I see no reason why the department should not do likewise. I have seen cases where mails have arrived in surburban districts two or three days after newspapers had been delivered by buses.
The only bus lines that can be utilized to advantage are those which run their buses on schedule. Such lines are utilized under contract where an improvement in the service can be brought about.
For first class mail?
For whatever mail is necessary to be carried between the particular points. It may not all be first class mail.

Has the experience of the department been that passenger and freight traffic by air is promoted by the use of the air mail service?
My information is that it does increase the traffic.

I do not know that I am familiar enough with the terminology of the department to elicit the information I desire, but as I understand the matter, a small post office does not come under the civil service. That is to say, such a postmaster would hire whatever help he might require and operate on a commission basis.
That is correct. The post office with a revenue of $3,000 or under would not come under the civil service commission.
What would be the revenue of the post office at Weyburn, Saskatchewan?
For the year ended March 31, 1935, it was $22,496.50.
Post offices with a revenue of $3,000 do not come under the civil service commission.
No; all those above $3,000 do.

Well, the post office at Weyburn does not. I wonder why. It is in the same position as a small post office; the postmaster merely receives a commission and he hires the help. Why is it not under the commission?

It is under
the commission in the matter of appointments. The $3,000 limit applies to the appointment of postmasters.

The postmaster at Weyburn may be appointed by the civil service commission but he hires the members of the staff and fixes their salaries. The office is not subject to the civil service commission. I submit that a post office with a revenue of S22.000 should be directly under the civil service commission.
That is quite arguable, I think. I cannot tell my hon. friend offhand the number of post offices with revenue approximating this amount that come under the commission.

Why is it that this post
office is not under the commission?

Of course
these offices are all inspected regularly. The reports are that the service in this particular post office is adequately performed by the present staff, and of course the service costs less than it would the other way.

I am gratified at the statement of the Postmaster General" that careful consideration is being given now to the trans-Canada air service. I was very much interested to hear the hon. member for Gloucester speak of the efforts he made to effect that. I know something at first hand of what he did, and I know that since his regime a good deal of water has flowed under the bridge, as I think the figures will show. Taking the air mail, there is an interesting comparison between the poundage carried in 1933 and in 1935. In 1933 there were 539,358 pounds, and in 1035, 1,126,084. The hon. member for Vancouver South spoke of the increase in passenger and other types of flying which very often accompanied the development of the air mail service. The figures I have taken from the report of the department of civil aviation really answer his question. For instance, although the air mail in pounds doubled between those two years, the amount of freight carried increased in a most extraordinary way. In 1933-these figures are for all Canada and of course go outside the mail service proper-there were carried by air 4,205,901 pounds of freight, and by 1935 that quantity had increased to 26,439,224, almost six times as much. The increase in passenger traffic between those two years was from 85.000 odd to 177,000 odd; and if the figures are followed right out one will find extraordinary increases all along the line, all of which goes to show that if you build up the air mail service you will build up the passenger and freight traffic.
As I understand the situation, it goes outside the department of the Postmaster General but it is something in which he is vitally interested, in his efforts to improve the postal service. I understand that there are under consideration plans which will involve the completion by March, 1937, of the ground services, airdromes, lighting and so on, from Winnipeg to Vancouver. Then, as to the prairie air services, which are in fairly good shape now but need reconditioning, parts having been abandoned-that is, the jump from Winnipeg east and west, to the mountains in the west and to the northern Ontario country in the east-that will involve a certain amount of installation of wireless in the mountainous sections and the completion of certain airdromes, and that work

Supply-Post Office
is well under way. I understand-I should like to have corroboration of this-that by the spring of 1938 the scene will be all set for a coast to coast air mail service. I am told that the run can be made in one day with machines in their present state of development, and at the present rate of progress we can expect something much faster by 1938. At any rate, at the present time the run from Halifax to Vancouver, can be made in twenty-four hours, or so I understand.
I would urge on the minister and on the government the extreme desirability of expediting this program if it can possibly be done. The airplane to-day is to the railway train what the railway train was to the oxcart one hundred years ago, and there never was a country on the face of the earth that needed a properly developed air service from coast to coast as this country does. It will do more to weld the west and the east together than anything else; and although, as the hon. member for Gloucester said, back in his day there was a certain degree of hesitancy in taking advantage of this service, I think that has been very much overcome. I believe the business world is more than ready for a daily service from coast to coast. I am convinced that it will grow from an air mail service to a modern passenger service. Of course air transportation as far as passengers are concerned is not a future possibility but a present actuality. One is far safer in the air on any standard line than on a highway in a motor car, no matter how good your driver on the highway may be; and one is very nearly as safe-I think the figures will show that one is actually as safe -flying with Imperial Airways or Pan-American Airways as one is in a train.
This country, because of its geographical situation, needs an air sendee as much as it needs anything. Consider also the future of the young people-young men and even young women-who have been learning to fly and who would be employed should the service be adequately developed. I know something about that at first hand because I had the honour to serve for some years on the board of directors of the London Flying Club, and for one year as its president, and I know the sacrifices that are being made by young Canadians in learning this new science. Last year London had the honour to be first in this respect in the dominion; we had ninety-one young pilots under instruction and we qualified seventeen. These young men are not the gilded youth of the town; most of them work for their living. They will come to the club and use the money they earn to take, perhaps,
one hour's instruction. You will not see them again for perhaps a month; they will be working and saving; then they will come back, and eventually they will qualify. That is happening right across the dominion, and with very little government assistance. A few years ago the system was that when a flying club acquired a plane the department would provide another plane equally good. That arrangement was done away with, and the present system is that the Department of National Defence will give one new plane every three years to a club which complies with certain conditions. If you have ever tried to teach young men to fly you will soon realize that one plane every three years does not go very far, because planes are fragile, and this means that these clubs have scraped along through the efforts of their members and of public-spirited citizens. That spirit has been displayed by flying clubs right across Canada, and justifies the Post Office, National Defence and every other department in getting behind this work, because the men in the ranks, if I may put. it in that way, have done their part and the government can and, I think, should do more. I believe I may say without offence that we had during the war the finest pilots in the world. We still have the same type of young men. They are making sacrifices to be allowed to take their part in this great means of transportation. Anything that the postmaster general can do along these lines will have my most hearty cooperation. I wish him Godspeed with this work.

Does the item under
consideration contain any appropriation for rural mail deliveries?

If my hon.
friend will look at the item under mail service he will notice "mail service by ordinary land conveyance, including rural mail delivery, 86,200,000."

I wish to protest against the present method of employing rural mail carriers. It is nothing less than a shame to ask people to tender for these positions and have them competing against each other with the understanding that the lowest tender will be accepted. That is the case at the present time, and it means that the department always has a man drawing the mail who has put the lowest value upon his own services. Why should this be when every other officer or employee of the department is appointed by the civil service commission? Take the caretaker who sweeps the floor and dusts and generally looks after a post office. A
Supply-Post Office

salary is set, applications are invited, and the civil service commission selects from among the applicants one who, they consider, is the best man. But when it comes to choosing a farmer to be employed on the rural mail the department says: Go to it, boys, we will give it to whoever will do the job the cheapest. I maintain that every rural route should be carefully gone over. Some are worth more remuneration than others. Take a rural route along a highway where t'he snow is ploughed oif in the winter time so that you can run a car. The service could be done more cheaply on that route than along a back-country road. A fair estimate of the cost per mile of running the rural routes should be placed upon each individual route, say $30, 840 or $50 a mile, as the case may be, for so many miles. Then let the department apply for contractors to carry the mail and have the civil service commission select a man who, they feel, is the best man to do it. To-day we are not getting the best class of men because we always take the lowest tenderer, the man who places the lowest value upon his own services. Many of these people are carrying mail to-day for less than it takes to feed their horses. That is absolutely wrong. I brought this point to the attention of the Postmaster General and of the Minister of Justice in the late government, and their answer was that at that time the finances of the country were not in a position to carry an extra burden. But I say that it is absolutely unfair to expect the rural people to be employed in this way and to make a discrimination against them in comparison with other employees of the department. I know the minister will realize the position and I ask him to take it into his serious consideration. I believe that the country at large is of the opinion that an injustice is being done under the present system of awarding rural mail contracts.
I should like to revent to my former question; but does the minister wish to answer the previous speaker's question?

A great many people entertain somewhat the same idea as has been expressed by the hon. member for Lanark with regard to rural mail carriers' remuneration. I cannot agree with him that this is something that should be left to the civil service commission, any more than I would agree that contracts for the erection of a building, which are now let by tender, should be placed under that commission. I think exactly the same principle applies to
[Mr Thompson.]
both. Unfortunately conditions in the country to-day are such that the tenders are very low. I regret that they are as low as they are, but that is because they are comparable with what men in the rural parts of Canada are receiving for similar services. I would say to my hon. friend that I know of no rural mail contract to-day which you would not be able to get many farmers in the district to carry on for the amount we are now paying.
Then my hon. friend suggested that we should set a minimum rate. I regret to say that these men obviously feel it is in their own best interests to carry the mail at the amounts of their tenders, and surely no man can complain very much if he gets the work at the price for which he offers to do it. My hon. friend knows what would happen in the rural districts to-day if legislation were enacted providing a rate for rural mail delivery out of all proportion to the amounts paid other people performing similar services in the district. Let me give a case in point. Tenders were called for not long ago in connection with a route for which, in the old days, there were usually six or eight applicants. In this instance forty-two tenders were sent in, many of them from the best farmers of that community. That contract was let for much less than the amount of the previous contract. As a matter of fact the highest tender was well below the amount of the former contract. But let me point out the great difficulty in saying that there should be a minimum amount per mile, and that contracts should not be let for smaller amounts. There may be just as much difference between the value per mile of two different mail routes as between the horses that are used to deliver the mail. There is a great difference in conditions in this country. In some parts we have snow for only a short time while in others we have snow for a much greater length of time. I appreciate my hon. friend's interest in the matter, and it is a question to which a great deal of consideration has been given by the department, but I do not see how we can devise any means that will give the people interested a fairer opportunity than they have at the present time, if the contracts are let fairly.

I cannot follow the minister's argument when he compares a rural mail contract with the contract for a public building. There is no comparison whatever. I venture to suggest that if the position occupied by the minister to-day were put up for tender many men would offer to do it for less.

Or my hon. friend's position.

Yes, or my own position. I ask the minister if he thinks this system is fair, at present when times are hard and farmers are trying to beat each other for these little jobs, taking them on for much less than they are worth. I know of two rural mail routes, with deliveries three times a week, which were tendered for last winter at the rate of eighty-seven cents a day. I said to the man, "Why, you are foolish. Why do you do it?" He replied, "Well, I am hard up. I have a boy at home and we have a horse there, and he can make that eighty-seven cents a day. It will be that much money coming in." I say it is absolutely wrong that people in this position should be asked to tender for these jobs. I agree with the minister when he says that different routes should command different prices. Some routes are much more difficult; road conditions vary, but an estimate could be made of the fair value per mile for any particular route. Tenders could be invited, and then either the minister or the civil service commission could select the very best man from among the applicants. To-day the lowest tender is accepted, which is the tender of the man who puts the lowest premium on bis own services.

There is just one word I should like to say with regard to a previous remark made by my hon. friend, though I am anxious to make some progress with my estimates. If my hon. friend thinks we are not getting at the present time a good service from the rural mail carriers he is under an erroneous impression, because my officials tell me that at this time, as a general rule, these men are rendering excellent service.

I want to say that I am in agreement with most of what has been said by the hon. member for Lanark in regard to these rural mail men. It is evident that the system now in existence is illogical and unjust. The government should set an example. We are trying to force those in industry and trade to pay their employees fair wages, and we are trying to stamp out cut-throat competition. The government should set an example by paying a decent remuneration to those who are in the service of the state, and by stamping out cut-throat competition among those who desire jobs or positions with the government. The trouble in regard to mail contracts is that very often people tender when they have no idea whatever of the value of the service. They may not have the remotest idea of what the work is worth, so they put in ridiculously low tenders and under the act the Postmaster General is bound to award the contract to the lowest tenderer, even though it may be absolutely out of proportion to the amount of work involved and the service to be rendered. I have been told that in days gone by it was possible to make some arrangement to avoid, in some measure, giving contracts to men who tendered at ridiculously low rates, but as a general rule I think it can be said that contracts are let to the low tenderers. Very often the low man has no idea of what the service is worth and he cuts the price, if I may so express myself.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering item No. 263, the outside service of the Post Office Department, 830,927,727.50.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was saying that the government should set an example in fair wages and fair competition, and I hope that the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) will take my remarks and those of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) into consideration and, when the financial conditions of the country permit, do something to improve the position of the rural postmen.
The point which was raised before six o'clock by the hon. member for Lanark is not a new one in this chamber. It has been raised, I think, at every session since I have been a member of the house. In 1929 it even formed the subject of a motion of want of confidence in the government, moved by the Hon. Mr. Guthrie, and we had a full dress debate upon it lasting two or three days. At every subsequent session the matter has been discussed and hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house have endeavoured to persuade the Postmaster General that something must be done for the under-dog, the rural postman, but we have not succeeded yet. I shall not take the time of the house to read the opinions which were expressed by hon. members, but as I said a moment ago from both sides of this chamber came expressions of opinion in favour of improving the conditions of the rural postmen. In the debate on the motion that was moved by Mr. Guthrie I might mention by name a few of the members who spoke in favour of the rural postmen: Hon. Mr. Guthrie; Hon. Mr. Stewart, the former Minister of Public Works; Mr. Anderson, representing one of the Toronto divisions; Mr. MacLean, representing Prince, Prince Edward Island; Mr. Jenkins, also representing Prince Edward Island, Mr. Pouliot, representing Temiscouata; Mr. Boyes, and Miss Macphail. With the permission of the house I think I might quote the opinion of one member who was loved by everybody in this chamber and who passed away only a few days ago. I refer to the late Mr. Spotton, who was one of the most genial members of the House of Commons, and I am sure that all of us who knew him regret very much his untimely death.

In the session of 1931 this question again came before the house. It will be remembered that one of the promises which were made by our friends the Conservatives during the 1930 campaign was to improve the lot of the rural postmen. Circulars were sent to postmen and rural mail carriers everywhere in the country, and it was promised that if they voted for the Conservative party, and that party were returned to power, something would be done to improve the conditions under which they worked. In the session which followed the change of government in 1930 the matter was brought up; some member of the house asked the then government if they were going to carry out the promise which they had made during the campaign to improve the lot of the rural postmen, and our friend the late Mr. Spotton on that occasion used words which I make my own. He said:
It is true, as the ex-Postmaster General has said, that a square deal for the rural mail carriers was advocated by many on this side of the house, and I suppose I really led in that matter. It seems too bad that of all the public servants in the Post Office department, the rural mail carrier is the only man who has, every four years, to tender for his position. The men in the city who to-morrow morning dons a suit of clothes paid for by the Post Office Department, walks around a few hours, goes out in the afternoon and walks around a few hours more, receives $1,409 or $1,500 and two suits of clothes a year and has a retiring allowance; but the fellow who hitches up the old mare and drives over the muddy roads or snowbanks gets the least consideration of all. I have advocated a square deal for these rural mail carriers. The exPostmaster General is correct when he says that this party is on record in this respect, and when the finances of the country become more buoyant, when the deficit in the Post Office Department is wiped out, wre shall look to the present government to give some relief to the rural mail carrier.
The Postmaster General has stated before in the house that it would take from four to five million dollars to bring the remuneration of the rural postmen up to thirty-five cents a mile, which is not an exorbitant figure.
Ten million dollars.

I do not remember
the figures exactly; I tried to find them in Hansard but I could not. It will require this amount to bring the remuneration of these rural mail carriers who perform a useful service for the state up to thirty-five cents per mile. I repeat that this is not an exorbitant figure. If that is true, it means that the

government of Canada is doing these men out of $10,000,000. Such a state of affairs cries out to heaven for relief. We should not allow these people who perform such a useful work to be so underpaid. I repeat again that in the matter of fair wages the government should set a good example and do something for these rural mail carriers.
It has been stated that the difficulty is the tender system. Certain people tender for contracts without knowing what they are worth and under the act the minister must award the contract to the lowest tenderer. If the Post Office Act needs amending, it should be amended. The Postmaster General stated that there was a great diversity in climatic and road conditions and geographical locations. That may be true, but I think it would be possible to classify these rural mail services into certain well defined classes. There are thousands of civil servants who vary according to competence, training and so on, and it is possible to grade these people according to their capacities and the work they perform. If that can be done with the tens of thousands of civil servants, I am sure it can be done with the rural mail carriers. It should not be any more difficult to grade and classify these services than it is to grade and classify the general civil service.
_ I hope the minister will give serious consideration to the plight of these men. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I agree almost entirely with what the hon. member for Lanark has said, but I dc not agree with him when he suggests putting these rural mail contractors under the control of the civil service commission. The civil service commission, the Civil Service Act and the so-called merit system are three of the greatest jokes in this country. The proof of this statement is the fact that whenever a new service is created, such as the national employment commission or the national harbours board, it is placed outside the control of the civil service commission. This shows that the government, whether Liberal or Conservative, have no faith in the so-called merit system, have no faith in the Civil Service Act and have no faith in the civil service commission. If the civil service commission and the Civil Service Act were working according to the intentions of those who framed the system, I would be the first to speak in favour of them. The fact is that more patronage and favouritism are to be found in the civil service now than existed before.
