The minister stated that the revenues from the Weyburn, Saskatchewan, post office amounted to about $21,000. What income would the postmaster receive from that post office?

He would
receive seventy per cent on the first $1,000, seventy per cent of the stamp revenue, thirty per cent of all revenue over $1,000 to $10,000 and twenty per cent up to $20,000. Since the committee rose at six o'clock I made an estimate of what that would be, based on the total revenue, and I find that it works out to a little over $6,000. This would pay the postmaster and his assistants. Perhaps 1 could answer another question, which I have no doubt the hon. member has in mind, as to why this is not a civil service post office. The fact that the revenue is over $3,000 would make this a civil service appointment, but it must first be graded in that way at the request of the officials of the the department. As long as that post office can be run as apparently it is being run, according to the reports of the inspector who visits the office from time to time, it is more economical to run it as a revenue post office and that is the reason why it is still being run in that way. It will still continue to be run as a revenue post office until a request is received from the department to have it put into grade 2B.

What revenue would
that post office have to return before it would be made a civil service post office?

That is quite an arbitrary figure. As- long as it is run as it is now being run, as long as the inspector reports the service as being satisfactory, theTe is economy in running it as a revenue post office. When it reaches a size which in the opinion of the department makes it advisable to place it in grade 2B, the request will be made to have it graded in that way.

I should like to urge
upon the minister the placing of that office under the civil service. What I am about to say is not meant as any reflection upon any person who has occupied the position of postmaster. The present incumbent of the office is retiring and the office is now practically vacant. The present system lends itself to a great deal of abuse. The postmaster need not be a resident of the city for a good part of the year; he can pay very low wages to his assistants with practically no holidays; he sets the hours which the staff
Supply-Post Office .

must work and yet may make more out of the post office than the entire staff combined. He may be absent for six or nine months in the year and never handle a single piece of mail. I am not casting any reflection upon any person, but I know this can be done; I know it has been done. I think it would be more satisfactory to the staff from the standpoint of the hours they would have to work, the holidays they would get, the pay they would receive and the service they would give, if the office was brought under the civil service.
I submit that for the consideration of the minister, particularly in view of the fact that the office of the postmaster in the Weyburn post office is to be vacant in the near future.

I support the hon. member for Weyburn, and I would ask the minister kindly to consider his request and do his best for the postmaster at Weyburn, paying him in sound money, because if he is paid in Aberhart money he will get nothing.
Does the hon. member for Temiscouata know where Weyburn, .Saskatchewan is?
I know, because it is in the district which is being flooded more than any other part of the country with false promises.

The statement has been made that with a view to increasing postal revenues there should be an increase in postage rates. I cannot agree with that suggestion. In my opinion the best way to increase the revenues of the post office is to reduce postage rates and give us the penny postage which we had after 1896 and again after 1921. I hope this government will give us that, for it has been proved in the past that the lower rate brought in a greater revenue. The same applies to post office boxes. Some years ago, in my town at any rate, the charge for the smaller box was SI and for the larger $1.50, and the rates were increased to S2 and S3 respectively, but instead of the revenue increasing it decreased and half the boxes are not used. What is the use of having boxes if the people are not using them? After all, the Post Office department is running a public service and in my opinion we are all wrong in increasing rates if we think this will result in increased revenues. This is true of customs tariffs; whenever you reduce the tariff you get an increased revenue and vice versa. I urge the minister to take this suggestion into serious consideration with his colleagues and give us the penny postage. The people are waiting for it.

In the first part of the item, salaries and allowances, I notice a decrease of almost $125,000. Does this mean that salaries of employees have been reduced or that there has been a reduction in the number of employees, or does it mean that the service will be curtailed to that extent?
It does not mean that salaries have been reduced; the onR1' reduction is the five per cent cut.
What is the minimum salary paid to male employees in the post office?

It depends of course on the range of employment, starting with the office boy, who gets $420 to $660, increasing $30 semi-annually for the first eighteen months and then $60 annually. It runs from there right up to the salaries of city postmasters which I gave the committee this afternoon. It all depends on the grade.

Some observations have been made this evening with reference to rural mail carriers. I sometimes wish that something could be done to do away entirely with this competitive system of awarding contracts and if at all possible to have men working on a permanent basis. I do not know whether it is possible to evolve such a scheme, but I hope the minister will take into consideration something of that sort, because I believe that in conjunction with the officials of the department it might be possible to work out a scheme whereby in connection with mail delivery in the rural areas the men would work for something approaching a decent living wage. I understand that in certain parts of the country the Post Office Department has abolished mail collection by the old method of horse and buggy and has adopted the use of automobiles. Has the minister any information with regard to that new method of collecting mail in some of the larger urban centres?

There are
only two places where the collection has been made by motor and that is in part of the Ottawa collection, and in Toronto which was done by officials in the service. In other cases it is left to the individual contractor to take mail from one point to another in such conveyance as he sees fit. It is quite apparent, however, that in a city like Montreal, in taking mail from the point of arrival to the point from which it is distributed some trucks should be used. A number of trucks are used to cover the distance. The rural mail carrier however can use, and in fact in a part of the season has to use, on a

Supply-Post Office
great many roads, horse and buggy and, for a part of the time, horse and cutter; frequently he uses a car if he can afford it and the roads lend themselves to the use of a car. There is no regulation.

I suppose it makes no difference to the Post Office Department whether they collect the mail by automobile or by horse and buggy, but those who can collect by automobile can tender so low as to wipe out all opportunity of the man with horse and buggy. From what the minister has said it appears that in Montreal and Toronto the department itself collects the mail. Am I right in that assumption? Is the collection in Toronto done by contract?

Most of it
is by contract but part of it is by motor service.

A motor service owned by
the Post Office Department?
Yes.

Is there any reason why
the department itself should not continue to operate its own collection agencies with its own motor vans which it has in different parts of the country?

There has
been a change in recent years. In a number of instances where formerly the department owned its trucks and had the service performed by men hired by the department, it is now letting to contractors who own their trucks carry on the service themselves. The department finds it is cheaper to let the contracts by tender than to buy the trucks and engage the men to service them.

Do I understand that it is
cheaper for the government to let these contracts by tender than to operate its own services?

That has
been the experience.

how long. I think a proper system of accounting could, with very little effort and very little delay, give parliament a full, concise and clear statement of the position of the department. It was shown this afternoon that there is an apparent surplus of $3,000,000. Would it be asking too much to request the minister to promise the committee at this time that he will assign some one in the department to the preparation of a proper financial statement showing the number of buildings which the government has, the actual cost of maintaining those buildings, and the interest charges on them? I think the information would be of value to the Post Office Department, in addition to giving us knowledge which we now lack. The minister stated this afternoon that it might be difficult to obtain this information because other departments occupy space in some of the post office buildings. It is true that in some of those buildings space may be taken by the Department of Public Works and the Department of National Revenue. But I should like to know why the Department of National Revenue should have space given it by the Department of Public Works when the former is a department which collects revenue. Is there any reason why the Department of National Defence, if it occupies space in these post office buildings, should not pay its share of the cost from its own appropriation?
It might take a few minutes to get the information, but, once obtained, it would be available for all time to come and could be supplemented or subtracted from as time and conditions might determine. So I make this appeal to the minister to put together for the benefit of the house and the country a proper statement showing the actual condition under which the Post Office Department is working from year to year.

As a new member, I should like to direct to the minister a question which, when answered, will enable me to avoid asking a lot of unnecessary questions. It has reference to the financial statement which has been read, and in which I am interested. In the reports of both the auditor general and the Postmaster General there is a large mass of information. On pages 6 and 7 of the report under discussion I find a general financial statement covering the year ' ended March, 1935. To my mind, at least, it is as clear as some of the financial statements issued by banks and other financial institutions. I find-to quote from this statement-that the net revenue for the year 193435 was $31,248,324.47, and that the expenditures for the same period were $28,974,316.53.
fMr. Heaps.]
In other words there was a profit of $2,274,007.94. This statement goes on to say that if the Post Office Department had been indemnified for the expenses imposed upon it through the franking privileges enjoyed by the various departments of government the revenue would have been increased by approximately $750,000, thereby increasing the surplus to the same extent. I see no reason why that sum should not be credited to the revenue account and charged up to the Minister of Finance. This report goes on to say that there is also a direct charge against the Post Office Department for carrying on savings bank business. This costs the department over $60,000 yearly, for which it receives no remuneration whatever, but its expenditure is increased by that amount. Again I see no reason why the Post Office Department should not be credited with that amount, which could be debited to the Minister of Finance.
The question I should like to ask at this time is this: Supposing there was added to the expense account an amount equal to the rents of the various buildings throughout the country, would that give a true picture of the financial situation of the Post Office Department? In other words, taking this mass of information which we find in the auditor general's report, plus the information in the Postmaster General's report, if we add to the expense account the amount chargeable to the Post Office Department for buildings, would that, in the opinion of the minister, give us a true picture of the whole situation?

That would be substantially so, I should think. I am not quarrelling greatly with either of the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken in regard to this matter. Of course these expenses and rentals for buildings were small matters in the early years, when this system was commenced, but they have grown to great proportions since that time. The hon. gentlemen said I had stated that this was an antiquated system, but I think he has in mind what someone else said. I say this is a system that has been in force practically since confederation. That may make it a little antiquated. As far as this statement is concerned, I think it is a fairly accurate statement-it is carefully audited-of the finances of the Post Office Department apart from any charge which might be made for the rental of the buildings and the services of the caretakers.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman who last spoke was in the committee when this question was discussed this afternoon, but we went into the matter at considerable

length at that time. I quite agree that it would be of value to this committee, particularly in times like these, to know as closely as we can get it-and we can get it fairly accurately-what this service costs. There is no question about that. There is, of course, the depreciation, which runs into many millions of dollars. There is the heating of ' all these buildings-

speechtext: The equipment.

Yes, the equipment, some of it very expensive. There is all the belting and all that sort of thing which is put into a building originally, and a great deal more which is put in subsequently. That is all supplied by the Department of Public Works and is not charged against the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And tractors.

Yes, there are tractors and a great many other kinds of equipment. I notice the alacrity with which my colleague the Minister of Finance refers to the enormity of that cost, and it is just possible that we have reached the time in the history of the finances of this country when we must take drastic steps to try to balance the departmental budget if this is to be reasonably close to a service at cost. From what I have heal'd in the chamber this afternoon it is quite apparent that the feeling of this committee is that in a department such as this, producing a revenue of $39,000,000 annually, we should not have too large a deficit as between actual revenue and actual cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There should be no
deficit.

The Minister of Finance tells me, as he has told me before very positively, that there should not be any deficit.
Sir	GEORGE	PERLElY:	Has	not	the
minister overlooked the fact that his department does a good deal of work for other departments without getting paid for it?

Oh, yes, there is no doubt about that.

hon. gentleman overlooked that fact?

An hon. member has just referred to the fact that it costs $750,000 a year for the franking privileges enjoyed by the various departments and by the different branches of parliament. There
is no question about that. I do not think the request that has been made is unreasonable, and I may say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North that after the committee met previously I asked the Department of Public Works if they would be able to furnish us with an estimate, as accurate as it could be made, of just what was the cost that has not been taken into account in the figures appearing in this statement. I think it is only fair to members of the committee that we should have that information, and in making that statement I am not criticizing the system which has prevailed in the past. Looking over the history of the Post Office Department for many years, I think it has had a creditable record. From time to time the postal rates have been changed, and in answer to my hon. friend from Kent, N.B., who wished to get back to two cent postage may I say that we can get back to two cent postage when the business of this country gets to the point where we shall be able to secure the revenue which will enable us to reduce the rates to that point. We cannot do that at the present time. It may be that we shall have to make a more strenuous effort to balance our budget than we have ever been required to make in the history of the department. The Minister of Finance tells me that we must do so, and I am satisfied he is right. In connection with the information for which I have asked, however, I am bound to say that I know the Department of Public Works is very, very busy at the present time, and my own department is equally busy. If any of my hon. friends visited any of the branches of the Post Office Department and saw how the employees are working, like bees in a hive, not only during the week but also on Saturday afternoons and very often on Sundays, during the session, I think they would be confirmed in the belief, which I think they hold, and which has been generally expressed this afternoon, that the employees of the department are working very hard.
With regard to having the accounts show exactly what the deficit is, I may say to my hon. friend that I shall endeavour to get an estimate, just as accurate as can be obtained, and shall be glad to show it to him and to discuss the matter with him at any time. If there are many other matters which hon. gentlemen wish to discuss I am afraid that discussion will have to be deferred until another time. I am bound to say that I am now trespassing upon the time that has been allotted to the Minister of National Health. I had hoped that we were about through,

I have one question
apropos of what the minister said this afternoon. He referred to air mail services, the majority of which were under contract. I shall
endeavour to get it.
On what basis are revenue post offices operated?

In the revenue offices the postmaster provides the assistants. The total pay, to cover the postmaster and his assistants, is seventy per cent on the first $1 ,000, thirty per cent of the stamp revenue up to $10,000, and twenty per cent on all revenue over $10,000. This item has been in the estimates for a long time. Shortly after the war it was urged upon the government of that day that it was extremely difficult for soldiers who had suffered injury to obtain employment in civilian life, on account of their disabilities. With that in mind arrangements were made whereby certain premiums were to be paid to insurance companies on workmen's insurance. At the present time nearly all the provinces have workmen's compensation acts, and the arrangement is that if an ex-soldier who suffers from some disability is employed and is injured owing to his disability, in certain cases there is a pension paid to the board or to the insurance company by the government.
There has been some question as to whether this is a very useful item, and at the present time I do not believe it does very much by way of procuring employment for ex-soldiers. Whatever good it may have been immediately after the war, it is not of very much use to-day, although it has been continued. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to bring a very serious matter to the attention of the minister, a matter relating to cancer. I should like to quote from a bulletin issued by the Vancouver Medical Association, dated June, 1935. The importance of this problem is
pointed out by Doctor Robb who states that this is the greatest of all public health problems. The bulletin reads:
Cancer is now second among all causes of death. The mortality is higher than that due to all infectious diseases combined (excluding pulmonary tuberculosis), and has ben rapidly increasing during the past ten years. During that time cancer has increased thirty-three per cent and tuberculosis has decreased twenty-five per cent. In 1920 there were 7,614 deaths from cancer in Canada, and in 1933, 10,646- an increase in the death rate from eighty-one to one hundred per 100,000. In 1933 one in every ten deaths was due to cancer. British Columbia is in an even worse situation as it has the highest cancer death rate of all the Canadian provinces. This has increased from 457 in 1924 to 836 in 1934 and there is almost an identical increase in Vancouver itself. There is a similar rise in mortality rates all over the world. The Metropolitan Life statistician thinks that 1933 may be the peak year but this cannot be accurately confirmed for several years to come.
This rise in mortality constitute the biggest problem facing organized medicine to-day and is the direct result of our failure to face the situation. Measures now available, if properly applied, would reduce the mortality to less than one-lialf the present figures.
Cancer differs from all other diseases in that there is no natural cure. There is but one opportunity to cure. This opportunity overlooked or ineffectively seized, the patient is doomed.
The point I want to bring to the attention of the government is the high cost of radium. While other cures are being tested, I believe the use of radium is the method most universally used. I have before me a newspaper article stating that the government of British Columbia is guaranteeing the pur chase of $105,000 worth of radium, about three or four grams. It has been stated to me by members of the medical profession that at the present time radium is in the hands of an international ring, and I suggest to the government that this should be investigated. The treatment of cancer is a very costly affair to those of moderate means and I bring this matter to the attention of the government in order that a thorough investigation may be made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Let me illustrate. Eno's Fruit Salts is advertised as fruit salts. In the United States the matter has been checked up and it has been proved that Eno's Fruit Salts is made of tar; it is made with citric acid from tar, and there is no fruit at all in it. It is not made with lemon or orange or grape juice or anything of that sort. In fact, in the United States the matter has been looked into and they had to change the libel 
-I mean the label. It may not be a libel to use that label in this country, but it is false representation and I wonder whether the matter could be checked. It is a real farce now. A druggist goes to this official and submits the formula of a cure-all of some kind. This is analyzed and then an entirely different product is made. I would ask the minister to get some bottles of Eno's Fruit Salts, so-called, from different druggists, and have the contents analyzed. And I suggest that this be done not only with this particular brand of salts but with all salts that are called fruit salts, in order to ascertain whether the people are being deceived or not. I submit that it is most important to have an analysis made.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Although I am not an expert on either fruit or salts, I am informed that the product mentioned by my hon. friend does contain fruit and salts, such as tartaric acid and citric acid, and therefore I imagine that this would be considered enough to give them the right to call it fruit salts. I frankly admit, however, that I am not sufficiently familiar with chemistry to discuss the matter with any degree of exactness, and if the hon. gentleman will make a complaint to the department with respect to any medicine or drug or product which he thinks is wrongly labelled, we shall be glad to have a complete analysis made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I thank the minister, but I would point out to him that while there may be some citric acid in the salts, there may be just a drop of lemon to a large quantity of tar, and tar is much better on the roof of a barn than in the human body. I lodge my complaint right now and I suggest that the minister should spend a few dollars to buy a dozen bottles of Eno's Fruit Salts in different drug stores and have it analyzed for the good of the country.

speechtext: Again I thank the minister, and after the explanation he has given I regret very much that Doctor Shields is not a doctor of law. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is it agreeable to the minister to discuss the Department of National Health under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Surely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are a few things I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, although 'he is probably aware of them. The first is that the Department of Pensions and National Health is really a department of pensions, national health practically playing no part. The Department of
2164	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
National Health was instituted in 1919 and was given a fair start. At that time its chief duties were the administration of the Food and Drugs Act, the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act, venereal disease control and child welfare. It is true there were other divisions, but these were by far the most important branches of the National Health department. The department still administers the Food and Drugs Act and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act-very important, I grant you- also the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act; but what seems to me, as a medical man of some thirty odd years standing, by far the most important features and functions of the Department of National Health, namely venereal disease control and the maternal and child welfare departments, have been dissolved and are, apparently, no longer factors in connection with the National Health department. Not only from a medical stand-aoint, but so far as the people of Canada ire concerned, the divisions of maternal and child welfare and of venereal disease control were far more important and far-reaching than any others.
When the department was instituted in 1919, largely in response to a luetic condition prevalent among soldiers and inmates of hospitals, the federal health department proceeded with a program in collaboration with the provincial departments and established a fund of $200,000 annually to be divided amongst the provincial governments for the control of venereal disease. In 1925, when it appeared that the government of Canada would withdraw this appropriation, interested parties busied themselves and made representations to the government, with the result that the amount was reduced to only $150,000. In 1926 it was cut to $125,000, and in 1927, to $100,000. During the administration of the last regime it was done away with altogether. Not only were the grants to provincial governments for the control of venereal disease withdrawn, but the departments of child welfare and venereal disease control were entirely abolished. The leader of the opposition, speaking on March 13, stated that the grants to the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, which is a voluntary medical association for the purpose of informing the public on matters pertaining to mental hygiene, the Canadian Tuberculosis Association, the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, and the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene, should be withdrawn and given to the provinces because the provinces w'ere in need of funds 
The right hon. gentleman was in power for five years, but during that period no moneys were devoted to the provinces for the control of disease. He was not long in office when the only grant the provinces were getting was withdrawn. This brought about a surge of protest from a number of the most important societies and associations in Canada. The Canadian Medical Association, the National Council of Women, the Canadian Pediatric Association, the Canadian Social Hygiene Council and the Canadian Public Health Aassoeiation all protested vehemently against the withdrawal of this grant. At their meeting in Toronto the National Council of Women resolved:
That representation be made to the Prime Minister regretting the discontinuance of the division of child welfare of the Department of Pensions and National Health.
Also:
That the Prime Minister or federal government he asked for a statement of policy of the Department of Pensions and National Health in relation to national health as a whole and in particular in relation to maternity and child welfare.
Tho national executive of the Canadian Social Hygiene Council resolved:
That in the opinion of the Canadian Social Hygiene Council the relinquishment by the dominion government of official leadership and responsibility for child welfare throughout the dominion is most regrettable;
And that as the true function of voluntary associations is to supplement governmental action, the delegation of an important part of the work of dominion department of health to a voluntary association is a retrograde step.
I will speak of that more fully a little later on. The Canadian Society for the Study of Diseases of Children, meeting in Brockville on June 1, 1934, passed the following resolution:
Be it resolved that in the opinion of the Canadian Society for the Study of Diseases of Children, the relinquishment by the dominion government of official leadership and responsibility for child welfare throughout Canada is most regrettable; and that as the true function of voluntary associations is to supplement governmental action, the delegation of an important part of the work to a voluntary association is a retrograde step.
This reference to a voluntary association, I believe, arises from the fact that when grants were withdrawn from the associations I mentioned in the first place, namely the Mental Hygiene Council, the Dental Hygiene Council, the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, and others, those grants were diverted to the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare, which was not a medical association

Supply-Pensions and National Health
at all but a purely voluntary association not under the control or supervision of medical authorities.
I am bringing these matters to the attention of the minister because, since our Department of National Health was instituted in 1919, it has been steadily dwindling. That has been true under two regimes; it is still on the dwindle, and unless the matter is given some serious thought and consideration by the present government the department might as well shut up shop and be discontinued entirely. If it is the opinion of this committee and the government that the Dominion of Canada does not need a National Health department, then there is no need to make a farce out of it; we might as well do away with it altogether as pretend to the people of this country that we have a National Health department when as a matter of fact we have not. As a medical man of the Dominion of Canada I am making my protest and bringing these matters to the attention of the minister for his consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman, who has given a great deal of thought to this question, explain to us in a few words his idea of the division of work between the provincial and dominion health authorities?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes. Ever since I have been in this house, for the last ten years, I have maintained that the federal government should lead in medical matters; that it should correlate the efforts of the provinces and lead the way in order to secure uniform services for all the provinces of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean in an educational way or to supersede the functions of the provinces?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, not to supersede the provinces but to control the provinces and bring about a uniform administration of health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In what way does the hon. gentleman suggest that the provinces could be controlled?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The provinces could be controlled very easily by the establishment of suitable grants. If such grants were made by the federal authority to the provinces, with the understanding that certain standards had to be conformed to and certain measures put into force, there is no question that the grants would be readily accepted by the provinces if this were made worth while by the dominion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I hesitate very much to
differ with my hon. friend from St. Boniface, but while I share his enthusiasm in behalf of public health I cannot altogether approve of that matter being brought under any department of the federal government. That was about the only thing which was done by .the former government and of which I approved, and I have often wondered whether I was wrong. I supported the action of the previous government in abolishing these grants; it seemed an unnecessary duplication of services. Why should we have a tubercular clinic controlled from Ottawa and another tubercular clinic controlled from Toronto? Neither do I approve of Toronto doctors coming to Ottawa and gathering voluntary subscriptions. Thousands of dollars are collected, without the books being audited, all in the name of national health. No doctor in Toronto should claim that name as his own.
I believe these matters should be dealt with in a businesslike way, and I do not approve voluntary organizations in relation to health. We have a right to protect the health of our people, but this should be done in a proper way. It may be every man's duty to see that it is done, but I believe it should be done under the provincial departments. Why, we might as well interfere with the provincial departments of education! Education is a very important question, but it does not come within the sphere of the dominion government. I consider that there is a great deal of unnecessary duplication. Can anyone imagine national health coming under the jurisdiction of a lawyer? That, in itself, is enough to condemn it from a federal standpoint.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I suppose if we were lawyers we would bring in -a judge to settle the matter. There is one thing I want to say to-night, and it is that the present system of national health is entirely and absolutely unsatisfactory. I agree that it should be either improved or discontinued, but I do not believe it can be discontinued. It would take a long time to go into the question fully, and I do not intend to do so to-night. I recognize that the present minister is a lawyer, but of course he is not to be blamed in any w'ay, particularly since he is a new minister, so I am not going to attempt to say anything that will embarrass him. But I want to say to him and to the government that this matter is of such vital importance that it should be given serious consideration, and that not later than a year from now, during the next session, we should decide to make drastic changes towards betterment, or we should decide to discontinue it and I do not think it should be discontinued. When I think of the people who have come into this country during past years, and of how little attention was given to the various physical and mental conditions, and when I look throughout the country and see what is taking place, I say that there was not given to examinations the attention which, in my judgment, should have been given, in connection with immigrants coming into the country.
I could go down a whole list of affairs which really should come under the Department of National Health but I am not going into that to-night. With regard to what the two hon. members have said about child welfare let me say that the usual procedure is that some voluntary organization undertake what they believe to be of interest, and if they can carry on that educational work to the extent where they establish some vital interest ip it, then it may be passed over to the Department of National Health, or to some provincial department. But to reverse the process and take an established department out of the Department of National Health of the dominion and leave it to some voluntary organization to carry on the work, not even under medical supervision, is certainly getting the cart before the horse. If there is anything like getting into reverse gear, then we surely have it in -that instance.

I say these few words merely to express my opinion, without arguing it. The matter is of such vital importance that it must be investigated, and changed one way or the other.

As I gathered from him, that matter and the one dealing with the child welfare branch were the two most important questions he had to bring to the attention of the committee, and because in his opinion these have been neglected he has suggested that the whole department should be abolished, but perhaps he was exaggerating.
As such, the department deals to a great extent with national and international obligations. For instance, there is the quarantine division; there is the food and drugs division which covers our obligations under the Geneva
convention respecting narcotics. In the past we have had a certain number of doctors attached to the immigration service, and may I point out to the hon. member that when these immigration examinations were being carried on the head of the department was himself a medical man, and if there was any fault to be found it would not be beyond the knowledge of the head of the department. When the branch dealing with child welfare was taken away from the department there was a distinguished member of the medical profession at the head of it. In the same way, when the venereal disease grant to the provinces was discontinued there was another distinguished member of the medical profession at the head of the department. So evidently any sins or crimes which have been committed by the department have behind them some medical knowledge and experience, and some medical reason possibly other than the ground of pure economy. I quote from the remarks which Doctor Beland, then minister in charge of this department, made in this house on July 18, 1924. He said:
When a grant for this purpose was first voted by parliament it was made clear that the appropriation would be only for five years at the rate of $200,000 per year. The first appropriation was only $100,000. For the second, third and fourth years $200,000 was annually voted. This vote is to complete the $1,000,000 which was intended to be appropriated in order to help the provinces in combatting venereal diseases. We were only called upon to appropriate $100,000 this year but representations were made to the government-to myself in particular-from the different provinces in favour of maintaining the vote as it formerly stood. We have cut the difference in two and are making the appropriation $150,000. The object of the appropriation in the first place was to enable the provinces to establish a service to combat venereal diseases. This was a new work and the provinces were called upon to furnish of their own money an equal amount, as they did After five years it is now found that the service is well organized throughout the country, and it is felt that the federal exchequer should not be called upon to pay as much money as it did before.
Nevertheless, as has been stated by my hon. friend, the appropriation continued to be made until 1931-32. I have received representations from a number of doctors to the effect that it would be a good thing if we could renew this appropriation or provide another.

Those in charge of the department within the last four or five years have in their wisdom decided that this work can be carried on just as well by voluntary organizations, but as my hon. friend informed us to-night-and he seemed to have good authority for what he said-it is perhaps not considered advisable by the great weight of medical opinion that private organizations should carry on this work. Quite frankly I cannot say from my experience up to the present that it would be preferable to have this money expended by the department itself rather than by this voluntary organization but I have no objection to studying the matter and taking the best advice I can get, and then possibly next year we may be in a position to please my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Not being a medical man I do not intend to express any opinions on the best way of handling this matter, but I would say from the experience

we have had in the last five years that this is one of the knotty problems of government. It is one of those questions which arise between the dominion and the provinces and which it is not easy to settle.
Last year it will be remembered that the then Minister of Pensions and National Health called a meeting at Ottawa of the representatives of the provincial health departments, and they had a very satisfactory meeting here. I know that Doctor Sutherland told me afterwards he had great hopes that some way would be found to coordinate their efforts to produce the best results possible. The object he had in mind at that time was to find some way in which the dominion and the provinces could cooperate in this very important work. The health of the people is something in which we are all vitally interested, and naturally medical men in this house have always discussed the question from that point of view because we all want to do what we can for the health of the people of this great dominion. There is nothing of greater importance, but it is in the first instance a provincial matter. The provinces are charged with that duty. This government has no power to make any regulations or to carry out any administration in regard to health anywhere in this country. We all know that.
Whether some plan can be found by which the federal Minister of Pensions and National Health can cooperate in a reasonable way with the health ministers and officers of the different provinces I do not know. Naturally the dominion would have to give some money for that purpose; this would1 be expected. But the efforts at cooperation that we have made from time to time in other fields in which the federal government as well as the provinces have an interest have not been very successful. We have tried to cooperate in a comparatively simple matter like the Companies Act, for instance, which is a much easier question to handle than that of health, but we have never been able to arrive at any conclusion or arrangement with the provincial authorities. I am sure that the present Minister of Pensions and National Health has it at heart to do anything he possibly can in a reasonable way to improve the health of the people of this great dominion, and I sympathize with him in the fact that there is great difficulty in connection with the provisions of the British North America Act, and in the fact that this federal parliament has no real authority to act unless the action is taken with the consent of the provinces. And so I think this question is one which

Supply-Pensions and National Health
requires a great deal more consideration before it is possible for anyone to suggest a plan that would be of any particular service in clearing up this rather knotty problem.

It is an appropriation for the enforcement of the regulations approved by orders in council of June 19, 1923 and February 25, 1930, concerning water for drinking and culinary purposes on vessels navigating on the great lakes and inland waters, and on common carriers engaged in international and interprovincial traffic. There is a constant supervision of vessels and cooperation with ship owners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Before this item is carried
may I state that I understand that there is an item for the Food and Drugs Act. It is not only Eno's Fruit Salts that I have to complain of, there is also the J. N. de Kuyper gin. On the label it is stated in big letters that it is distilled in Holland, which is untrue. It is made in Montreal. It is a kind of concoction made of syrup that they mix with alcohol. I wonder whether the minister will not take steps to have the label rectified, so that people will not be under the impression that they are drinking pure Holland gin when they have only that concoction made of syrup by a liquor company in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am almost inclined to share my hon. friend's indignation at the thought that J. N. de Kuyper gin, which was a staple in the province of Quebec some years ago, has deteriorated. If such is the case I shall most certainly make such inquiries as I can in order that it may be brought up to the standard which we were led and taught to expect from that great concern.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Thank you. There is
something else. In the United States they have a wonderful publication which indicates the cost of patent medicines to the producers. For instance there is Vapex, which is sold at around SI a small bottle, and it costs the producer about twelve cents. It is an exploitation, of the public, and if the facts were made known to the Canadian people there would be much less of such exploitation by the makers of medicines.
TSir George Perley.l

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I had the pleasure of reading the same book as my hon. friend has read. I think it is called a Hundred Million Guinea Pigs, and reference is made in it to the matters to which he has drawn my attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is almost as bad as the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: According to A Hundred Million Guinea Pigs, the book to which my hon. friend refers, the poor people of the United States of America were being deluded, through heavy advertising, into buying worthless preparations. But I am informed that the regulations of the Department of National Health provide that if a commodity or a product is required to be registered and the price of the product is found away in excess of its real value, registration is refused.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does that mean that when they ask for registration the department demands to be shown the cost? Is that what is done?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I understand that an estimate is made from the formula. The application form states the price.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And the cost price too?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It states the sale price, and
the department makes a careful study of the cost price.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Therefore there will be a great saving in our drug stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There is a matter which
lies outside the scope of the inquiry of the special committee, but which I think should receive the attention of the minister. I refer to the circumstances of a large number of imperial service men wh,o are in Canada and who were not domiciled here at the outbreak of the war. Their needs are dealt with, of course, through the Canadian representative and the Canadian office of the British Ministry of Pensions. Nevertheless circumstances are such at the present time that their needs are being referred to various municipalities, and in the constituency which I represent a number of municipalities have had reason to complain, feeling that these men should be dealt with by the Canadian government. It has been difficult to explain the situation, and it has been difficult also, in referring the matter to the Canadian Office, to secure a review of their claims such as we usually secure from the Canadian

Supply-Pensions and National Health
pension commission. I should like to ask the minister if he has considered the advisability, in view of the vast array of often disgraceful evidence as to the condition of these men, of making suitable representations to the British Ministry of Pensions that these men may secure redress.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The matter to which my
hon. friend refers was brought to-day to the attention of the committee on pensions, although it came up indirectly in connection with another matter; the representations covered the point raised by my hon. friend. The request of those representing the imperial veterans is that they be treated on exactly the same basis as Canadian veterans. At the present moment, as my hon. friend knows and as doubtless the committee is aware, soldiers who served in the imperial army but who were domiciled as citizens of Canada prior to the war are treated on the same basis as Canadian citizens, in that the pension which is granted to them by Great Britain, and which is very often below that which is granted by Canada, is augmented to the Canadian level. The point now raised is whether persons who have come to Canada since the war and who did not serve in the Canadian forces, but served in the imperial forces, shall receive the same treatment as those who served in the Canadian forces. The question is a difficult one to settle. As my hon. friend well knows, it is one for negotiation as far as possible with the British Ministry of Pensions. In any case I should be very glad to take the point up again with the British government, though I understand it has been discussed many times, as to whether they are prepared to make an additional allowance to their soldier pensioners now residing in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Before this item is carried would it be possible to know how many veterans in armies other than the British army had the preference over Canadian citizens in the civil service. I wonder whether the minister can answer that, or if he cannot, would he be kind enough to tell me from what department I can get that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I will, with great pleasure,
refer my hon. friend to the civil service commission.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend
(Sir George Perley) is satisfied I will hold open item 173. The hon. member for Davenport suggested that perhaps item 175 could
be passed at once. There are two large items, one for $2,600,000, the other for $3,000,000. I am quite willing to leave the $3,000,000 item open and pass the one for $2,600,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think
it makes any difference.

Item agreed to.
Unemployment assistance, $2,600,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
What imperial veterans are
eligible for assistance under this particular item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Those who arrived in
Canada prior to 1924 and who are pensioners or who have commuted their pension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is there any reason why
that date should not be carried forward, for the benefit of men who arrived after 1924?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I think it would be rather
a big question to discuss at this late hour. I assume that the regulations were made in 1924 and they took the situation as it was found at that time. No government since then have thought that their duty lay in looking after imperial soldiers of another country. They took the situation as they found it at that time, and since then no government have considered it to be their duty to look after soldiers of another country. As a matter of fact, as my hon. friend knows, these men are being looked after by the municipal authorities of the municipalities in which they reside. They are not starving.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Unemployment assistance, as I understand it, is assistance given by this government to ex-service men in lieu of the ordinary relief which is given by the municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is given to small pensioners who are unemployed. Only small pensioners are in receipt of it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: To all pensioners who are unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: To unemployed small pensioners whose pensions are not sufficient to bring them up to the scale laid down by the department as the scale they should receive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What would be involved if that date were carried forward to January 1, 1936?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have not the faintest idea and I do not think we could get an estimate of it, because I do not think there are any figures available anywhere to let us know how many British ex-soldiers have migrated to Canada since 1924.
2174	.	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Could that information be obtained from the municipal relief lists?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It might be obtained in some way. I am in hopes that if a classification of ex-service unemployed is made by the veterans' assistance commission all these facts and figures will be available, but certainly they are not available now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I suppose the dominion
government is now paying a large share of the cost of relief for these men, in any case?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What amount of assistance do these men get? Is it on a sliding scale?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is a basic rate of $18.75 per month for a single man. The basic rate was laid down in the famous Hyndman report, and it is now in effect. It increases for a married man and for pensioners with children. If their pension is less than the municipal rate of relief we supplement it in order to bring it up to the municipal rate or to this basic rate of $18.75 per month for a single pensioner; $30 per month for a pensioner with one dependent, $34 per month for a pensioner with two dependents; $39 per month for a pensioner with three dependents, and so on. For a pensioner with seven dependents it is $51 per month. As an incentive to the pensioner to endeavour to secure employment casual earnings up to $10 per month are not deducted, and the earnings of any child living with the pensioner are exempted up to $40 per month.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the rank of the ex-service man make any difference at all in the scale?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, not at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What amount was expended last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Last year we expended
$2,042,000, and as a result of the findings of the Hyndman commission the amount will be considerably increased this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Does the minister expect to have to spend $2,600,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Because of the increase recommended in the Hyndman report?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that returned men get this relief providing they are already receiving a small pension, in order to bring it up to a certain amount, or do they have to be on relief in the municipality in which they reside in order to have their income supplemented in this way?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The returned soldier who is a pensioner has no connection with the municipality at all as far as relief is concerned; he is not obliged to apply to the muni ipality. He applies to this department, and if his income is not as high as this basic rate or as the rate of the municipality in which he lives, then we supplement that amount. So far the government of Canada has not considered it to be its duty to look after exsoldiers who are not pensioners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have in mind a pensioner who is receiving a small pension; no doubt the minister will recall the case, because I have spoken to him about it. I think this man has a pension of about $30 per month, and he has a family of four children. He strenuously objects to applying for relief,, either from the municipality or under this scheme, and I was just trying to get it clear as to whether he should be on municipal relief.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: If he receives a pension of $30 per month he would probably have that amount brought up to the scale I mentioned a few moments ago.

Item agreed to.
War veterans' allowances, $3,200,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I would like some explanation of this increase, but it is almost eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It will not take me a moment to explain. The war veterans' allowance was introduced in 1930. At that time a very good estimate was made as to the annual amount that would be expended, and the estimate has been pretty closely followed since then. As the soldiers grow older and reach the age of sixty more of them come under this act. Some of them grow less capable of looking after themselves and also come under the act. That is the reason for the increase.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is a reasonable explanation, but I should think their numbers would be growing less.

Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Not in this particular
category. There are more reaching the age of sixty than are dying. In 1930 it was anticipated that by 1959 the expenditure under this item would reach $12,000,000 annually.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is this allowance made only to those over sixty?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: To those sixty or over or to those holders of small pensions who are permanently incapacitated.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
